title: Your push was rejected — a teammate got there first
summary: A real origin and a real teammate clone. They push, you push, git says no. Understand what non-fast-forward means and fix it without a force push.
mental_model: `origin/main` is not the server. It is your local memory of where main was on the server the last time you looked. `fetch` updates that memory. `pull` is fetch plus merge. A push is rejected when your memory is stale — you would be erasing commits you have never seen.
danger: The tempting fix is `git push --force`. On a shared branch that deletes your teammate's commit from the server. `--force-with-lease` refuses to do exactly that, which is why it should be your default if you force at all.

commit.message: Ramp the pump instead of slamming it on

steps.title: See what you think the world looks like
steps.why: Your local main has your ramp commit. origin/main still points at the initial commit, because nothing has told your clone otherwise. That gap is the whole scenario.

steps.title: Try to push
steps.why: Rejected: non-fast-forward. Git will not move the server's branch to a commit that does not contain the server's current commit — that would silently delete your teammate's work.
steps.expect: ! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first). Exit code 1 is the point.

steps.title: Fetch — look, do not merge
steps.why: `fetch` downloads the new commits and moves origin/main. It touches nothing you are working on. This is the safe first move every single time, and the reason experienced people rarely type `pull`.
steps.expect: Your branch and origin/main have diverged, 1 and 1 different commits.

steps.title: See exactly what they did
steps.why: Before combining histories, read the other side. `origin/main...main` with three dots shows the commits unique to each. Reviewing this takes ten seconds and prevents most bad merges.

steps.title: Rebase your commit on top of theirs
steps.why: Rebase replays your commit as if you had written it after theirs, producing a straight line. Their commit is untouched; yours gets a new sha. Safe here because your commit has never been pushed anywhere.

verify.label: your work sits on top of theirs, as a single commit
verify.hint: git fetch origin, then git rebase origin/main

steps.title: Push, this time as a fast-forward
steps.why: Now your main contains origin/main, so the server can simply slide its pointer forward. No force, no lost work, no argument.

steps.title: Confirm on the server itself
steps.why: origin.git is a real bare repository on disk. Reading its log proves this was never a simulation — both commits are genuinely there.

contains: Ramp the pump instead of slamming it on
verify.label: the server has both your commit and your teammate's
verify.hint: fetch, rebase onto origin/main, then push

verify.label: nothing was lost or duplicated on the server — exactly three commits
verify.hint: if you see more, you merged where a rebase was intended; if fewer, a force push ate a commit

verify.label: your local branch is in sync with origin/main

pitfalls: `git pull` defaults to a merge, which sprinkles 'Merge branch main of ...' commits through history. `git pull --rebase` (or `git config pull.rebase true`) avoids that.
Never rebase a branch other people have already pulled — you rewrite shas they are building on.
`--force-with-lease` refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen. Plain `--force` does not check. Prefer the former, always.
`git fetch --prune` deletes remote-tracking branches for branches deleted on the server; without it, `git branch -r` fills with ghosts.
cheatsheet: update your memory of the server, change nothing else
commits you have that the server does not
commits the server has that you do not
replay your work on top of theirs
fetch then rebase, in one step
force, but refuse to erase unseen commits
